topics.title: The Writing Process
topics.short: Writers prewrite, draft, revise, edit and publish, and they go back and forth between the steps as needed.
topics.trouble: Learners think revising means fixing spelling. Revising changes the ideas, the order and the support; editing fixes errors in sentences.

topics.title: Purpose and Audience
topics.short: Before you write, ask why you are writing and who will read it. Both shape what you say and how you say it.
topics.trouble: Learners write only for the teacher, so they leave out information a real reader would need, or use a tone that doesn’t fit.

topics.title: Finding and Narrowing a Topic
topics.short: Brainstorm, list, freewrite or cluster ideas, then narrow the topic to one you can cover well in the space you have.
topics.trouble: Learners choose a topic far too big for the length (“the history of sports” in two pages).

topics.title: Topic Sentences
topics.short: A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph, usually as the first sentence.
topics.trouble: Learners write an announcement (“This paragraph is about dogs.”) or a small detail as the topic sentence.

topics.title: Supporting Details
topics.short: Facts, examples, reasons and details support the main idea of the paragraph.
topics.trouble: Learners add details that are true but off the point, or restate the topic sentence in new words instead of supporting it.

topics.title: Paragraph Unity
topics.short: Every sentence in a paragraph supports its one main idea.
topics.trouble: Learners keep an interesting sentence that drifts from the main idea.

topics.title: Transitions
topics.short: Transitions show how ideas connect: time (then, later), addition (also), contrast (however), cause and effect (therefore) and example (for instance).
topics.trouble: Learners use a transition that signals the wrong relationship (however where the idea continues), or start every sentence with one.

topics.title: Organizing a Paragraph
topics.short: Arrange details in an order the reader can follow: by time, by place, by importance, or by comparison.
topics.trouble: Learners list details in the order they thought of them.

topics.title: Concluding Sentences
topics.short: A concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph’s idea without just repeating the topic sentence.
topics.trouble: Learners copy the topic sentence word for word, or bring in a new idea at the very end.

topics.title: Narrative Writing
topics.short: A narrative tells events in order, from a point of view, with characters, a setting, a conflict and a resolution.
topics.trouble: Learners summarize events (“then this happened, then that happened”) instead of building a scene the reader can see.

topics.title: Showing and Telling
topics.short: Show a feeling with action, dialogue and sensory details, and tell when a quick summary moves the story along.
topics.trouble: Learners name every feeling (“She was scared”) where actions would show it, or are told never to tell; good writing does both.

topics.title: Descriptive Writing
topics.short: Use precise nouns, strong verbs and sensory details, arranged in a clear order.
topics.trouble: Learners stack adjectives (“the big, huge, giant tree”) instead of choosing one precise noun or verb.

topics.title: Expository Writing
topics.short: Expository writing explains or informs, with facts, definitions and examples, in a neutral voice.
topics.trouble: Learners slip their own opinions into writing that is meant to inform.

topics.title: Ways to Explain
topics.short: Explain by definition, classification, process, compare and contrast, or cause and effect.
topics.trouble: Learners mix structures in one paragraph without signal words, so the reader can’t tell how the ideas relate.

topics.title: Facts, Opinions and Claims
topics.short: A fact can be checked. An opinion is a belief or a judgment. A claim is a statement an argument sets out to prove with reasons and evidence.
topics.trouble: Learners treat a strongly worded opinion as a fact, or think a fact they agree with proves an opinion.

topics.title: Persuasive Writing
topics.short: Persuasive writing takes a position and gives reasons and evidence to convince a reader.
topics.trouble: Learners give opinions without support, or attack the other side instead of making a case.

topics.title: Thesis Statements
topics.short: A thesis states the main point or claim of an essay, in a sentence or two, and the whole essay supports it.
topics.trouble: Learners write a topic (“This essay is about the Civil War”), a question, or a plain fact as a thesis.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Theses
topics.short: A strong thesis is specific, can be argued or explained, and can be supported in the space you have.
topics.trouble: Learners choose a thesis too broad to support, or too obvious to need an essay.

topics.title: Outlining
topics.short: An outline puts the thesis, the main points and their support in order before you draft.
topics.trouble: Learners skip the outline, or write one whose points don’t each support the thesis.

topics.title: Introductions and Hooks
topics.short: An introduction catches interest, gives the reader the context they need, and leads to the thesis.
topics.trouble: Learners open with a dictionary definition or a sweeping claim (“Since the beginning of time…”).

topics.title: Body Paragraphs
topics.short: Each body paragraph has a topic sentence tied to the thesis, evidence, an explanation of the evidence, and a link to what comes next.
topics.trouble: Learners drop in evidence without explaining how it supports the point.

topics.title: Conclusions
topics.short: A conclusion returns to the thesis in new words and shows why it matters, without starting a new argument.
topics.trouble: Learners repeat the introduction word for word, or start a brand-new point.

topics.title: The Five-Paragraph Essay
topics.short: An introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion: a starting form that teaches how an essay holds together.
topics.trouble: Learners force every topic into exactly three points, even when it has two or five.

topics.title: Growing Beyond Five Paragraphs
topics.short: Let the argument decide the number and order of paragraphs: longer sections, a paragraph for the other side, and conclusions that do more than restate.
topics.trouble: Learners treat the five-paragraph form as the definition of an essay, so their writing can’t grow with harder subjects.

topics.title: Kinds of Evidence
topics.short: Facts, statistics, examples, expert testimony and anecdotes: each kind has strengths and limits.
topics.trouble: Learners treat one story, an anecdote, as proof of a general claim.

topics.title: Using Quotations
topics.short: Introduce a quotation, quote the words exactly, cite the source, and explain what the quotation shows.
topics.trouble: Learners drop a quotation in with no introduction, or end the paragraph on it without explaining it.

topics.title: Summarizing
topics.short: A summary gives a source’s main ideas in your own words, much shorter than the original, without your opinions.
topics.trouble: Learners retell every detail in order, or add what they think of the source.

topics.title: Paraphrasing
topics.short: A paraphrase restates one passage in your own words and your own sentence structure, about as long as the original, with a citation.
topics.trouble: Learners swap in a few synonyms but keep the source’s sentence structure (patchwriting). That still borrows the author’s writing, and it counts as plagiarism.

topics.title: Avoiding Plagiarism
topics.short: Give credit for other people’s words and ideas: quotation marks for exact words, and a citation for anything you quote, paraphrase or summarize.
topics.trouble: Learners think a citation is needed only for direct quotations, or that facts everyone knows (common knowledge) need one.

topics.title: Judging Sources
topics.short: Check who wrote it and what they know, the evidence they give, the date, the purpose, and whether other good sources agree.
topics.trouble: Learners trust a source because it looks professional or comes first in a search.

topics.title: Research Questions
topics.short: Turn a topic into a focused question, find several good sources, and take notes that record where each idea came from.
topics.trouble: Learners search for one fact instead of asking a question that needs several sources to answer.

topics.title: Citation Styles and Their Uses
topics.short: MLA (9th edition, 2021) is used in literature and the humanities, APA (7th edition, 2020) in psychology and the social sciences, and Chicago (18th edition, 2024) in history and publishing.
topics.trouble: Learners mix styles in one paper, or follow an older edition’s rules.

topics.title: MLA Works Cited Entries
topics.short: MLA builds each entry from core elements in order: author, title of source, title of container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, publication date, location.
topics.trouble: Learners leave out the container (the website, journal or book that holds the piece), or italicize the article’s title instead of the container’s.

topics.title: MLA In-Text Citations
topics.short: An MLA in-text citation gives the author’s last name and the page, with no comma: (Morrison 45).
topics.trouble: Learners add a comma or “p.” inside the parentheses (Morrison, p. 45), which belongs to other styles.

topics.title: APA References and Citations
topics.short: APA uses author and date: (Lee, 2020, p. 12) in the text, and reference entries that begin Lee, A. B. (2020).
topics.trouble: Learners capitalize every word of an article or book title in an APA reference. APA uses sentence case there: only the first word, the first word after a colon, and proper nouns.

topics.title: Chicago Notes and Bibliography
topics.short: Chicago’s notes-and-bibliography style uses numbered footnotes or endnotes and a bibliography; Chicago also offers an author-date system.
topics.trouble: Learners use Ibid. everywhere. The 18th edition prefers shortened notes and allows Ibid. only for the source of the note just before.

topics.title: Reading a Citation
topics.short: Pick out the author, the title, the container, the publisher, the date and the pages in a citation in any style.
topics.trouble: Learners confuse the title of an article with the title of the journal or website that published it.

topics.title: Revising for Ideas and Order
topics.short: Revise by adding, cutting, moving and replacing: check the thesis, the support, the order and the clarity.
topics.trouble: Learners only fix sentences and never ask whether a paragraph belongs or is in the right place.

topics.title: Giving and Using Feedback
topics.short: Useful feedback is specific, kind and something the writer can act on: name what works, then one or two things to try.
topics.trouble: Learners give vague praise (“Good job!”) or vague criticism (“This is confusing”) instead of a specific suggestion.

topics.title: Editing and Proofreading
topics.short: Edit for grammar, punctuation, spelling and format. Read slowly and aloud, or on paper, to see what you wrote and not what you meant.
topics.trouble: Learners proofread on screen at reading speed, so their eyes fill in what they meant to write.

topics.title: Cutting Wordiness
topics.short: Cut words that add nothing: “due to the fact that” → “because,” “in my opinion, I think” → “I think.”
topics.trouble: Learners pad their writing to reach a word count, which makes it harder to read.

topics.title: Formal Letters
topics.short: A formal letter has the sender’s address, the date, the inside address, a salutation, the body, a closing and a signature, usually in block format.
topics.trouble: Learners use a friendly letter’s tone and closing (“Love,”) in a formal letter, or leave out the inside address.

topics.title: Writing a Clear Email
topics.short: A clear subject line, a greeting, the main point first, short paragraphs, a polite closing and your name.
topics.trouble: Learners bury the request at the end, or leave the subject line blank.
